States cannot nullify constitutional provisions they dislike; they can only nullify unconstitutional federal laws. The segregationist misuse of nullification no more discredits the principle than abusive police conduct discredits law enforcement itself.

A Necessary Restoration

Reviving nullification would not create "50 separate countries." It would restore federalism's proper balance. States would decline enforcement of specific unconstitutional laws, not all federal authority. Interposition creates political crises that force national reconsideration—exactly what occurred in 1833 and what the Founders intended. The threat of state resistance disciplines federal overreach, encouraging Congress to stay within constitutional bounds.

The alternative is continued descent into centralized, unaccountable bureaucracy—the very tyranny the Revolution opposed. As Jefferson warned, "When all government, domestic and foreign, in little as in great things, shall be drawn to Washington as the centre of all power, it will render powerless the checks provided of one government on another." We have reached that precipice.

Conclusion: Reclaiming Our Revolutionary Legacy

The American Revolution was itself an act of nullification—colonies declaring Parliament's laws void and unenforceable because they violated fundamental constitutional principles. The Constitution was meant to preserve this spirit of liberty under law, not domesticate it. State nullification is not a threat to the Union; it is the mechanism that makes the Union worth preserving. It embodies the Founders' wisdom: that freedom is safest when power is divided, that local self-government is essential to liberty, and that no government can be trusted to limit itself.

The doctrine stands as a constitutional, historical, and moral imperative. States must reclaim their sovereign authority to judge constitutional limits and to protect their citizens from federal overreach. The alternative—unquestioning submission to an all-powerful central government—represents not constitutional fidelity but its betrayal. Nullification is not rebellion; it is the Constitution's final defense. And in an age of federal omnipotence, it is a defense we cannot afford to abandon.

Thirteen pre-existing sovereign polities—each with its own constitution, government, and people—chose to delegate certain limited powers to a new federal government.

This “compact theory” was not fringe; it was a widely accepted way of understanding the federal arrangement at the founding. Key points:

  • The Preamble says, “We the People of the United States” in a context where each state ratified separately; the people of each state assented to the compact through their conventions.
  • Ratification occurred state by state, not via one national referendum. Each state could have refused.
  • The federal government’s powers are enumerated and limited; the states retain all powers not delegated.

If the Constitution is a compact among political communities, then each party to that compact must retain some capacity to judge its terms—especially when another party (the federal government) claims new powers beyond those agreed upon.

2. The Tenth Amendment’s reservation of powers

The Tenth Amendment crystallizes this logic:

> “The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.”

This is not a mere tautology. It codifies the principle that the federal government is a government of limited, enumerated powers, whereas the states are governments of general jurisdiction, constrained primarily by their own constitutions and by specific prohibitions in the federal Constitution.

If the federal government can unilaterally expand its own powers, interpret its own authority without meaningful check, and impose its will on reluctant states in all matters, then the Tenth Amendment is reduced to empty rhetoric. State nullification is one mechanism by which the reservation of powers in the Tenth Amendment gains practical force.

II. Jefferson and Madison: Intellectual Roots of Nullification

Nullification is frequently dismissed as an extremist theory, yet its intellectual roots trace back to two of the most important architects of American constitutionalism: Thomas Jefferson and James Madison.

1. The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions of 1798

In response to the Alien and Sedition Acts—federal laws that criminalized certain criticism of the government and prolonged residency requirements for immigrants—Jefferson and Madison drafted the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, adopted by those states’ legislatures.

Jefferson wrote in the Kentucky Resolution:

> “That the several States who formed that instrument [the Constitution], being sovereign and independent, have the unquestionable right to judge of its infraction; and that a nullification by those sovereignties, of all unauthorized acts done under color of that instrument, is the rightful remedy.” (Kentucky Resolutions of 1798, emphasis added)

Madison, in the Virginia Resolution, spoke of a state’s duty to “interpose” to arrest the progress of unconstitutional federal actions. He was more cautious in his terminology, but the thrust was similar: the states were not mere provinces; they were guardians of the constitutional balance.

2. The logic of “interposition” and “nullification”

The logic is straightforward:

  • The Constitution is a compact of limited delegation.
  • The federal government is one creature of that compact, not its sole interpreter.
  • If that creature claims powers never granted, it breaches the compact.
  • The sovereign states, as parties to the agreement, have a right and duty to protect their citizens from that breach.

Nullification, in this sense, is not a call for disorder; it is a structured constitutional response to federal usurpation, intended to preserve the rule of law as originally understood, not to destroy it.

III. Federalism as a Safeguard of Liberty

1. A divided sovereignty

The framers did not trust concentrated power. The separation of powers within the federal government (legislative, executive, judicial) is one check; federalism—division of power between national and state governments—is another.

Without a meaningful mechanism by which states can resist federal aggrandizement, this second safeguard is hollow. A federal government that can:

  • define the scope of its own powers,
  • enforce its own interpretation,
  • and prevent states from saying “no”

is effectively supreme in all things, contrary to the structure the Constitution was meant to establish.

2. States as guardians of local values and diversity

Nullification protects the function of states as laboratories of democracy and as repositories of local culture, priorities, and policy preferences.

  • Different states have different demographics, economies, and values.
  • A uniform, centralized policy may be ill-suited—or actively harmful—to many of them.
  • State nullification allows a state to say: “This federal policy is not only unconstitutional, but fundamentally at odds with our obligations to our citizens; we will not enforce it here.”

Historically and today, when Washington enacts broad, one-size-fits-all schemes, many states have seen them as infringements on their autonomy, whether in areas like education, health regulation, drug policy, gun control, or surveillance. Nullification offers a way to maintain meaningful diversity in law and governance.

IV. The Supremacy Clause and Why It Does Not Obliterate Nullification

Critics often point to the Supremacy Clause (Article VI) as the definitive refutation of nullification. The Clause reads:

> “This Constitution, and the Laws of the United States which shall be made in Pursuance thereof; and all Treaties made, or which shall be made, under the Authority of the United States, shall be the supreme Law of the Land…”

The key phrase is “in Pursuance thereof.”

1. Only constitutional acts are supreme

The Supremacy Clause asserts that laws made in pursuance of the Constitution are supreme. It does not say all federal statutes are automatically supreme, regardless of their constitutionality. If Congress enacts a law that exceeds its enumerated powers, that law is, in principle, no law at all—a usurpation, not an act “in pursuance” of the Constitution.

Nullification is precisely the stance a state takes when it says:

  • “This particular federal act is not in pursuance of the Constitution; therefore, it is not truly supreme over our laws.”

Under this view, nullification is not a denial of the Supremacy Clause; it is a defense of it against federal acts that fail its condition of being constitutional.

2. Judicial review is not the only guardian

It is true that the Supreme Court has claimed the authority of judicial review, the power to declare laws unconstitutional. But even accepting judicial review, it does not logically follow that the Court is the exclusive and infallible arbiter of constitutionality.

  • The Constitution nowhere explicitly grants the Court a monopoly on constitutional interpretation.
  • All branches take oaths to support the Constitution; they share responsibility for interpreting it.
  • States, too—through their officials—take oaths. When federal actions trample the Constitution, state officials cannot simply shrug and say, “Only the Supreme Court may object.”

Nullification insists that constitutional fidelity is not the private preserve of nine justices; it is the duty of all constitutional actors, including state governments.

V. Modern Echoes of Nullification: Interposition in Practice

Even in an era when the term “nullification” is disfavored, the practice of states refusing to cooperate with federal policy is widespread and often celebrated—especially when it aligns with a state’s political leanings.

1. The anti-commandeering doctrine

The Supreme Court itself has affirmed that the federal government may not “commandeer” state resources to enforce federal policy. In cases like New York v. United States (1992) and Printz v. United States (1997), the Court declared:

  • Congress cannot force state legislatures to enact federal regulatory programs.
  • Congress cannot compel state executive officials to administer or enforce federal schemes.

This means a state may constitutionally decline to participate in enforcing certain federal laws. While this is not full nullification (since the federal government may still enforce its laws directly), it is a close cousin: it affirms that states retain real power to obstruct overreaching federal policies by non-cooperation.

2. Sanctuary jurisdictions

Cities and states that declare themselves “sanctuaries” for certain immigration practices effectively refuse to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement. Whether one agrees or disagrees with their policy objectives, these jurisdictions are engaged in a form of nullification in everything but name:

  • They view certain applications of federal immigration law as unjust or harmful.
  • They decline to expend state resources enforcing them.
  • They often pass local policies that, in practice, frustrate federal enforcement.

Defenders of these sanctuary policies argue for state and local autonomy and for a moral duty to protect residents from what they regard as federal overreach. This is the nullification impulse at work: the belief that states should not be passive conduits for any policy the federal government chooses to impose.

3. Marijuana legalization and other policy areas

States that have legalized marijuana—medical or recreational—have effectively nullified federal drug prohibition within their borders. Federal law still lists marijuana as a Schedule I substance, but:

  • States license growers, distributors, and retailers.
  • State and local police generally do not enforce federal marijuana laws against those acting in accordance with state law.
  • The federal government’s practical ability to enforce its own law without state cooperation is limited.

Again, regardless of one’s personal stance on drug policy, this is a clear example of states treating a federal policy as unacceptable and shaping their own legal environment accordingly. This practice exists because the states still retain sufficient sovereignty to resist federal directives in meaningful ways.

VI. Nullification as a Peaceful Check, Not a Path to Chaos

A frequent critique is that nullification invites anarchy or disunion: if every state can declare federal laws void, what stops the Union from dissolving into a patchwork of conflicting jurisdictions?

This objection mischaracterizes both the doctrine and the alternatives.

1. Nullification as structured resistance

Nullification is not a blanket claim that states can ignore any federal law they dislike. A robust doctrine would require:

  • A clear constitutional argument that the federal law exceeds delegated powers or violates rights.
  • A formal act by state institutions (legislature, governor) declaring the law inoperative within the state.
  • Open, not secret, resistance—subject to public scrutiny and political accountability.

Through this process:

  • The dispute is brought into the open.
  • Citizens can debate both the state’s position and the federal policy.
  • Political pressure may compel Congress to amend or repeal the contested law.
  • Other states can join or oppose the nullifying state, creating national dialogue rather than quiet acquiescence.

This is more transparent and accountable than silently allowing the federal government to stretch its powers, hoping that courts alone will occasionally rein it in.

2. The alternative: Centralized power with no real check

Without nullification or something like it, the federal government effectively becomes the judge of the extent of its own powers—a situation James Madison explicitly warned against as the very definition of tyranny.

  • Congress claims a power.
  • The executive enforces it.
  • The federal courts, composed of federal officials, interpret it.
  • States must submit, with no effective recourse other than constitutional amendment—a nearly impossible process on controversial issues.

In practice, this creates a ratchet effect whereby federal power expands and rarely contracts. Federal agencies and Congress steadily accumulate authority, while states become mere administrative subdivisions. Nullification is a way to reverse that ratchet and reassert the original federal balance.

VII. Answering Historical Objections: Nullification and Its Misuses

Critics often point to some of the darkest episodes associated with claims of state sovereignty—most notably, the defense of slavery and later resistance to civil rights—as reasons to reject nullification entirely.

1. Misuse does not invalidate the principle

Any constitutional mechanism can be abused.

  • Free speech has been invoked to defend vile and hateful rhetoric.
  • Due process has been used to thwart legitimate criminal prosecution.
  • Judicial review itself has been used to uphold unjust laws (Plessy v. Ferguson) or strike down beneficial ones.

The fact that a principle has been invoked in unjust causes does not mean the principle is inherently invalid. The proper response is to apply it correctly, not to discard it.

2. Nullification as a protector of rights, not only powers

State nullification can serve liberty-enhancing ends. For example:

  • A state might refuse to cooperate with federal surveillance programs it believes violate the Fourth Amendment.
  • A state might decline to enforce federal gun restrictions it believes infringe the Second Amendment.
  • A state might shield its residents from federal policies that overstep bounds in health, education, or environmental regulation.

In all these instances, nullification is used not to oppress, but to protect individual rights against an overbearing central authority. The moral character of nullification depends on its content and purpose, not its form.

VIII. A Call for Reviving Nullification as a Constitutional Ideal

Under modern doctrine, courts have rejected the strongest forms of formal nullification. But constitutional meaning is not frozen by judicial fiat. Citizens, scholars, and lawmakers retain the ability—and responsibility—to advocate for a constitutional order that better protects freedom and federalism.

Reviving nullification as a constitutional ideal would:

  1. Reassert that the federal government’s powers are limited and delegated, not unlimited.
  2. Encourage states to take their role as guardians of liberty seriously, rather than acting as mere administrative arms of Washington.
  3. Promote healthy political conflict and debate over the boundaries of federal authority, rather than passive acceptance of every new program or mandate.
  4. Restore a balance in which the federal government is strong where it must be (e.g., national defense, interstate commerce properly understood) but constrained where it ought to be (local governance, community standards, experimentation in policy).

Nullification is not a panacea and must be exercised carefully. But without some meaningful state power to say “no”—to declare that a federal policy is beyond constitutional bounds—the American system drifts toward a consolidated, national government unchecked by the very states that created it.

If we take the Tenth Amendment seriously, if we believe that sovereignty ultimately resides in “We the People” of our several states, and if we recognize the dangers of concentrated power, then the doctrine of state nullification is not a radical threat to the Constitution. It is a logical and necessary extension of the federalism the Constitution was designed to protect.

State nullification is the claim that a state has the constitutional authority to declare a federal law “null and void” within its borders if the state believes the law is unconstitutional. While this doctrine is not accepted under modern constitutional law, its supporters advance a fairly consistent set of reasons and claimed benefits.

Below is a structured summary of those reasons and supposed benefits, from the perspective of proponents.

1. Theoretical basis supporters rely on

a. “Compact theory” of the Union

Proponents often start from the idea that:

  • The Constitution is a compact among sovereign states (or among “the peoples of the several states”), not a one-way grant of authority to a supreme national government.
  • Because the states voluntarily joined this compact, they retain some ultimate authority to judge whether the federal government has exceeded its delegated powers.

Under this view, when the federal government acts outside the powers granted to it, it isn’t just wrong—it’s acting ultra vires (beyond its authority), and its acts are not truly “law” at all. State nullification is then framed as a way for states to refuse to recognize unconstitutional assertions of power.

b. The Tenth Amendment and limited, enumerated powers

Supporters heavily invoke the Tenth Amendment:

> “The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.”

They argue:

  • The federal government’s powers are limited and enumerated; most governing power remains with the states.
  • Nullification is a practical “enforcement mechanism” to make that reservation of powers meaningful.
  • Without some state-level veto or resistance, the federal government can gradually reinterpret its own powers expansively (through Congress and the federal courts), slowly eroding the very federalism the Tenth Amendment was meant to preserve.

c. States as guardians of liberty

In this framework, states are not merely administrative units of a centralized state, but coequal political societies. Proponents claim that:

  • States have an obligation to protect their citizens’ rights against unconstitutional federal intrusion.
  • Nullification is an act of interposition—the state government “standing between” the federal government and its people to shield them from unconstitutional acts.

Historically, this idea appears in:

  • The Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions (1798–99), associated with Madison and Jefferson, resisting the Alien and Sedition Acts.
  • Later theories of John C. Calhoun during the Nullification Crisis (South Carolina vs. federal tariffs).

2. Supposed benefits: limiting federal power

a. A direct check when other mechanisms fail

Supporters argue that ordinary checks on federal power are often weak:

  • Elections: National elections may be dominated by large states or national coalitions that ignore regional interests.
  • Courts: Federal courts are part of the federal system itself; asking them to limit federal power is, in their view, like “asking one branch of Washington to police another.”

They claim nullification:

  • Provides a bottom-up safeguard: states can refuse to enforce or recognize a law they see as unconstitutional, rather than waiting for a court case to be brought and decided (which may take years or never happen).
  • Creates an immediate brake on federal overreach, especially where the federal law affects a state’s core functions (policing, education, internal commerce, etc.).

b. Preventing constitutional “mission creep”

Another claimed benefit is that nullification:

  • Counters the tendency of federal powers (like the Commerce Clause or the Spending Power) to expand over time through broad interpretations.
  • Forces a public, political confrontation whenever Washington pushes into areas that states consider reserved to them.

In this view, without nullification, the division of powers is essentially policed only by the federal government itself—and thus likely to drift steadily toward centralization.

3. Supposed benefits: protecting state sovereignty and local self-government

a. Preserving the federal balance

Proponents see federalism not as a technical detail but as a core liberty-protecting structure:

  • Multiple centers of power (state and federal) make it harder for any one government to become oppressive.
  • States, as distinct political communities, have their own constitutions, traditions, and values; nullification lets them defend those against national homogenization.

Nullification is said to:

  • Help keep the federal government confined to truly national concerns (foreign policy, interstate commerce, etc.).
  • Preserve meaningful state autonomy over schools, policing, land use, health policy, and other traditional state domains.

b. Respecting local diversity and experimentation

Supporters often tie nullification to a “laboratories of democracy” idea:

  • Different states have different cultures, economies, and policy preferences.
  • A one-size-fits-all federal policy may be ill-suited or deeply unpopular in certain regions.

State refusal to enforce a federal policy is seen as:

  • A way to preserve policy diversity in a large, heterogeneous country.
  • A means to encourage policy experimentation: if a federal mandate is resisted by several states, it can provoke debate and lead to alternative models at the state level.

(Modern examples people point to as “nullification-like,” even if not formally labeled as such, include state-level marijuana legalization in defiance of federal drug laws, or state “sanctuary” policies on immigration enforcement.)

c. Keeping government closer and more accountable to the people

Supporters claim state governments are:

  • Closer to citizens: easier to access, more visible, and more responsive to local concerns.
  • Less insulated than distant national institutions that may be influenced by national media and interest groups.

Nullification is framed as:

  • A way for a community’s immediate representatives (state legislators) to say, “This national law is intolerable to our people and our understanding of the Constitution.”
  • A form of local self-government, allowing communities to govern themselves on contested issues rather than being ruled by national majorities.

4. Supposed benefits: protecting minority regions and rights

a. Shielding regional minorities from national majorities

In a large republic, regional or cultural minorities can be outvoted and overruled at the national level. Supporters argue that nullification:

  • Gives such regions a defensive tool against policies that deeply offend local moral, economic, or constitutional views.
  • Helps prevent federal legislation that might heavily burden some regions to benefit others (e.g., tariffs, regulations that favor certain industries or regions).

From their perspective, without something like nullification, a national majority can:

  • Use federal power to systematically disadvantage some states or regions.
  • Dictate social and economic arrangements to local communities that vehemently reject them.

b. A peaceful alternative to secession or rebellion

In theory, nullification is presented as a middle route between passive obedience and violent resistance:

  • Rather than revolting or seceding, a state simply refuses to enforce or recognize the contested federal law.
  • This can force negotiation, compromise, or constitutional amendment without immediately breaking the Union.

Supporters sometimes argue that:

  • If the only options are “obey everything Washington does” or “leave the Union,” the system invites extreme outcomes.
  • Nullification gives a structured way to express profound constitutional disagreement while still remaining in the Union.

5. Supposed benefits: forcing constitutional dialogue and clarification

a. Triggering national debate about constitutional limits

When a state formally declares a federal act unconstitutional or refuses to implement it, supporters say it:

  • Raises public awareness of constitutional boundaries that might otherwise be ignored.
  • Forces Congress, the executive, the courts, and other states to directly confront the disputed issue instead of letting it slide by default.

This can lead to:

  • Negotiated adjustments in federal law or enforcement.
  • Eventually, Supreme Court clarification or even constitutional amendment if the disagreement persists.

b. Checking judicial supremacy

Many nullification advocates are skeptical of the idea that the Supreme Court has the final and exclusive power to say what the Constitution means:

  • They see this as “judicial supremacy,” as opposed to “constitutional supremacy.”
  • They argue that each branch of government, and each level of government (state and federal), has a duty to interpret the Constitution within its sphere.

From this vantage point, nullification:

  • Reasserts that states are co-interpreters of the Constitution, not subordinates who must accept whatever the Court says.
  • Counters the risk that a small number of federal judges could effectively rewrite the Constitution through expansive interpretations.

6. Practical forms of “nullification” supporters envision

In practice, even advocates rarely imagine a state literally “voiding” a federal statute in the sense of making it disappear. Instead, they envision:

  • Non-cooperation: a state declines to use its officers, resources, or institutions to enforce a federal law (e.g., refusing to help enforce federal gun laws, drug laws, immigration rules).
  • State-level protections: passing state laws or constitutional provisions that protect certain liberties or limit cooperation with federal programs.
  • Symbolic resolutions: legislative declarations that a federal act is unconstitutional, used to mobilize political opposition and litigation.
  • Interposition through courts: state courts interpreting federal and state constitutions in ways that limit the practical reach of federal laws within the state (subject to preemption and federal supremacy, but still a potential friction point).

Supporters argue that the federal government often depends heavily on state cooperation to administer and enforce its laws; refusal to cooperate is thus a powerful functional check, even short of open confrontation.

7. A brief note on status and controversy

  • Under modern Supreme Court doctrine, formal nullification—states declaring federal law void and legally disregarding it—is unconstitutional.
  • However, some related behaviors (especially anti-commandeering, where states refuse to use their own resources to enforce federal law) have been partially validated (e.g., Printz v. United States, Murphy v. NCAA).
  • The doctrine’s history is heavily contested and often tied to deeply problematic causes (most infamously, defense of slavery and resistance to civil rights), even though some nullification-like claims have also been invoked to resist widely criticized federal laws (e.g., the Alien and Sedition Acts, fugitive slave laws).

Supporters see nullification or nullification-adjacent strategies as a constitutional firewall against federal overreach and as a way to preserve meaningful state sovereignty and local self-government in a large, diverse republic. Critics respond that it undermines national unity and the rule of law, but those critiques are distinct from the reasons and benefits supporters claim for the doctrine.

A Helpful Field Guide to People Who Hate State Nullification

If you’ve ever suggested that maybe—just maybe—states don’t have to roll over every time Congress sneezes out another 2,000-page bill, you’ve probably met them:

The Anti-Nullification Purity Brigade.

Anti-nullification critics insist that states absolutely cannot refuse to enforce federal laws…
…unless it’s a law they don’t like.

  • When states ignored federal marijuana prohibition:

  • When “sanctuary cities” refuse to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement:

  • When a state says, “We’re not enforcing this federal gun law / mandate / regulation”:
    “UNCONSTITUTIONAL REBELLION! THIS IS THE CIVIL WAR 2.0!!!”

Apparently, “states’ rights” is one of those quantum terms: it exists, doesn’t exist, and is morally good or evil depending solely on the policy preference of the person screaming on cable news at that moment.

Ask them why states shouldn’t nullify anything, and their answer boils down to this:

> “Because the federal government said so.”

The same federal government that:

  • Couldn’t build a functional healthcare website with a billion dollars and a decade’s notice.
  • Loses track of trillions of dollars, but will audit you for getting your mileage wrong.
  • “Accidentally” spies on its own citizens, then assures you it was all just an oopsie.

But somehow, when it comes to constitutional limits and individual rights, that same crew of professional committee-sitters and lobbyist-whisperers becomes a council of infallible philosopher-kings whose every statute descends from Mount Olympus.

States questioning them?
Unthinkable. Treasonous. Possibly terrorism.

Sure, Washington makes mistakes sometimes—like… well… everything—but don’t worry, the solution is always:
“Give them more power and less resistance.”

3. “But the Supreme Court Said…” (The New Priesthood)

Anti-nullifiers have a simple theology:

  • The Constitution is whatever five lawyers in robes say it is.
  • Those five lawyers may completely change their minds 20 years later.
  • Both versions are equally “settled law” and unquestionable truth.

If you point out that nullification is, among other things, a way for states to say, “No, we’re not enforcing this,” they respond:

> “You can’t do that! That would undermine the Supreme Court!”

Yes. That’s the point.

Without nullification or some form of state resistance, the federal government gets to:

  1. Declare its own powers.
  2. Interpret its own declarations.
  3. Enforce its own interpretations.
  4. Tell you resistance is illegal because it says so.

It’s a beautiful, self-contained system—if you’re the one in charge of it.

4. They Love “Democracy” (As Long As It’s Far Away)

Nullification critics love to recite this phrase with great moral gravity:

> “We can’t have 50 different policies. That would be chaos.”

Translation: “We can’t have people in different places deciding things for themselves. That would undermine my dream of a perfectly uniform nation in which everyone is equally regulated and equally miserable.”

They’ll say:

  • “We need national solutions to national problems.”
  • “We must act together as one.”

And by “we,” they mean:
“People who live 1,000 miles away from you, don’t know your town exists, and will never deal with the consequences of what they’re forcing you to do.”

When it comes to abortion, gun laws, environmental rules, drug policy, healthcare—you name it—the message is the same:

> “Democracy is sacred… but only if it’s exercised through one capital city, over 330 million people, in a one-size-fits-none manner. Anything less is dangerous fragmentation.”

Letting California be California and Texas be Texas?
“That’s insane!”
Forcing Texas to be California and vice versa?
“Responsible governance.”

Say “nullification” in front of certain people and watch them break the land-speed record for historical cherry-picking.

“There was a Civil War, you know!” they whisper, as if you were unaware.

To them, the entire legal, political, and moral question is settled by shouting:

  • “SLAVERY!”
  • “CIVIL WAR!”
  • “YOU CAN’T DO THAT, IT’S LIKE THE 1850s ALL OVER AGAIN!”

Never mind:

  • States nullifying federal fugitive slave laws to protect escaped slaves?
    That actually happened. Nullification against oppression.
  • Modern states refusing to enforce federal drug or gun laws?
    Also nullification. But if the result isn’t politically convenient, back to the “Civil War!!!” talking point.

Critics treat history like a Netflix series they half-watched while scrolling Twitter: they remember a few dramatic scenes, forget all nuance, and assume yelling “SLAVERY” ends any discussion about federalism until the end of time.

This is a favorite:

> “If states can resist federal power, what if they nullify GOOD laws?”

Deep question. Let’s also consider:

  • If people can speak freely, what if they say dumb things?
  • If you can own a kitchen knife, what if you make bad soup?

They argue:

  • Since some states might nullify laws we like, we should ensure no state can nullify any laws.
  • In order to prevent theoretical misuse, we should maintain a system where misuse of power by the federal government is absolutely guaranteed and impossible to escape.

In their minds, the only safe world is one where:

  • No one close to you has real political power.
  • Every serious decision affecting your life is made far away, by people you’ll never meet, serving interests you’ll never see, elected with money you’ll never have.

But don’t worry. It’s for your safety.

Ask an anti-nullifier where exactly the Constitution says states must enforce every federal edict without question. Watch the gymnastics:

  • “Well, there’s the Supremacy Clause…”
    Which says federal laws made in pursuance of the Constitution are supreme.
    Who decides what’s “in pursuance”?
    “The federal government. Obviously.”

  • “But the courts said…”
    So the federal government decides if the federal government is overstepping, and if it says “Nope, all good,” that’s the end of the conversation?

  • “That’s how it works!”
    According to… the people it benefits most. Shocking.

The Doctrine of State Nullification: A Constitutional Safeguard Against Federal Tyranny

“When the government becomes a monster, the people have the right to revolt.” These words, echoed by Thomas Jefferson, capture the essence of a doctrine that has been both revered and reviled throughout American history: state nullification. Nullification is the principle that individual states possess the constitutional authority to declare federal laws unconstitutional and void within their own borders. Far from being a extremist notion, nullification is a vital component of the federal system envisioned by the Founding Fathers—a system designed to prevent the concentration of power and protect the liberties of the people. In an era where the federal government routinely oversteps its enumerated powers, the doctrine of nullification is not only constitutionally sound but also a necessary defense of states’ rights and individual freedom.

I. The Constitutional Foundation: The Tenth Amendment and Enumerated Powers

The Constitution establishes a federal government of limited, enumerated powers. All powers not expressly granted to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people. This principle is enshrined in the Tenth Amendment: “The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.” The amendment makes explicit that the federal government’s authority is confined to the specific powers listed in the Constitution—such as regulating interstate commerce, declaring war, and coining money. Any action beyond these delegated powers is an usurpation of state sovereignty.

Nullification is the logical mechanism to enforce this division of authority. If the federal government passes a law that exceeds its constitutional bounds, the states, as the original parties to the constitutional compact, have the duty to interpose and prevent the enforcement of that law within their borders. Without such a check, the federal government could effectively rewrite the Constitution through mere legislation, eroding the very foundation of limited government.

II. The Constitution as a Compact Among Sovereign States

The notion that the Constitution is a compact among the states is not a fanciful interpretation; it is rooted in the historical context of the ratification process. The Constitution was drafted by delegates sent by the states, and its adoption required the consent of nine states, as stipulated in Article VII. The language of the document itself repeatedly refers to “the United States” as a collection of states (e.g., “The Senate of the United States shall be composed of two Senators from each State”). The Federalist Papers, especially those written by James Madison and Alexander Hamilton, describe the federal system as a union of sovereign states, each retaining its inherent authority except where specifically delegated.

This compact theory implies that the states are not subordinate to the federal government; rather, they are its creators. As parties to the compact, states retain the ultimate right to judge when the federal government has breached the terms of the agreement. This principle was famously articulated in the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions of 1798–1799, authored by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison respectively, in response to the Alien and Sedition Acts. Jefferson wrote that “the several states composing the United States of America are not united on the principle of unlimited submission to their general government,” and that when the federal government assumes undelegated powers, “a nullification of the act is the rightful remedy.” Madison similarly argued that states have the duty and right to interpose to stop constitutional infringements. These resolutions laid the intellectual groundwork for nullification as a legitimate state power.

III. Nullification as an Essential Check on Federal Overreach

The doctrine of nullification is not a mere theoretical abstraction; it is a practical necessity. The system of checks and balances among the three federal branches—legislative, executive, and judicial—was designed to prevent tyranny within the federal government. However, when all three branches collude to expand federal power beyond constitutional limits, the states become the last line of defense for liberty.

Consider the concept of judicial review, established in Marbury v. Madison (1803). While the Supreme Court has the authority to strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution, this power is not explicitly granted by the Constitution itself. Moreover, the Court is a part of the federal government; there is no guarantee that it will always act as an impartial arbiter of constitutional limits. History is replete with examples of the Court upholding governmental overreach—Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) and Korematsu v. United States (1944) being particularly notorious. In such instances, the states must have the means to protect their citizens from unconstitutional federal actions. Nullification provides that means.

Without the threat of nullification, the federal government would hold a monopoly on constitutional interpretation, able to expand its own powers without effective restraint. The Framers understood this danger. In Federalist No. 46, Madison assured that the state governments would serve as a barrier against federal encroachments, noting that “the state governments… will have the same advantage… in protecting [their] rights, which the federal government has in protecting the rights of the people.” Nullification is the ultimate expression of that protective barrier.

IV. Addressing Counterarguments: The Supremacy Clause and Judicial Authority

Critics of nullification often point to the Supremacy Clause (Article VI) as evidence that federal law is always supreme. However, the clause states: “This Constitution, and the Laws of the United States which shall be made in Pursuance thereof… shall be the supreme Law of the Land.” The critical phrase is “in Pursuance thereof.” Federal laws are supreme only when they are enacted pursuant to the Constitution. If a law exceeds the powers granted to Congress, it is not in pursuance of the Constitution and therefore is not supreme. Nullification merely restores the proper order by refusing to enforce an unconstitutional act.

Another common objection is that the Supreme Court has the final say on constitutionality, and that nullification undermines the rule of law. Yet the Constitution does not explicitly grant the Court the power of judicial review; that doctrine was a judicial creation. Moreover, even if judicial review were accepted, it would not preclude states from exercising their reserved powers. The Tenth Amendment explicitly reserves powers to the states, including the power to interpose against unconstitutional federal actions. The Supreme Court itself has recognized state sovereignty in many contexts (e.g., New York v. United States, 1992). To deny nullification is to deny the states any meaningful role in preserving the constitutional balance.

Some argue that nullification leads to anarchy and disunion. However, the doctrine is not a call for secession or lawlessness; it is a legal remedy to be employed with caution, reserved for clear cases of federal overreach. The Nullification Crisis of 1832, often cited as an example of the dangers of nullification, actually demonstrates its effectiveness as a check. South Carolina nullified a federal tariff, leading to a confrontation that was resolved through compromise and the eventual reduction of the tariff. The episode showed that nullification can initiate negotiation and prevent tyranny, not disunion.

V. Modern Applications: Nullification in the 21st Century

Nullification is not a relic of the past; it is alive and well in contemporary America. In recent years, numerous states have passed laws effectively nullifying federal mandates they deem unconstitutional. For example, many states have legalized marijuana in defiance of the federal Controlled Substances Act, arguing that the federal government lacks authority to regulate intrastate activity. Similarly, several states have enacted “Second Amendment sanctuary” laws, refusing to enforce federal gun control measures they view as infringing on the right to bear arms. These actions reflect the enduring relevance of nullification as a tool for states to protect the rights of their citizens.

Even the Supreme Court has begun to acknowledge limits on federal power, as seen in cases like United States v. Lopez (1995) and National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius (2012), where the Court struck down federal laws for overstepping the bounds of the Commerce Clause. These rulings validate the core concern of nullification: the federal government must operate within its enumerated sphere. Nullification serves as an additional, more immediate safeguard when the courts are slow or ineffective.

VI. Conclusion

The doctrine of state nullification stands as a bulwark against the relentless expansion of federal power. It is deeply rooted in the Constitution’s structure, the historical understanding of the Union as a compact, and the fundamental principle that government derives its just powers from the consent of the governed. In an era where the federal government often acts as if its authority is unlimited, nullification offers a vital mechanism for states to defend their sovereignty and the liberties of their people. To reject nullification is to acquiesce to an ever-growing central Leviathan, one that the Founders would scarcely recognize. Embracing nullification is not an act of rebellion; it is an act of fidelity to the Constitution and the rule of law.

This essay argues that nullification, properly understood, serves as an essential constitutional safeguard protecting state sovereignty and individual liberty against federal overreach.

The Constitutional Foundation for Nullification

The Compact Theory of the Constitution

The Constitution emerged not as a national decree but as a compact among sovereign states. When the states ratified the Constitution, they delegated specific, enumerated powers to the federal government while retaining all others. As parties to this compact, states necessarily retain the authority to judge when the federal government has exceeded its delegated powers. James Madison, the "Father of the Constitution," articulated this principle in the Virginia Resolutions of 1798, asserting that states, as sovereign parties to the constitutional compact, must possess the means to prevent violations of that compact.

The Tenth Amendment explicitly confirms this arrangement: "The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." This amendment isn't merely declaratory; it establishes a constitutional presumption in favor of state authority and against federal encroachment.

The Absence of Federal Supremacy in Ultra Vires Acts

While the Supremacy Clause establishes that constitutional federal laws supersede state laws, this supremacy extends only to laws "made in Pursuance" of the Constitution. An unconstitutional federal law, being void ab initio, cannot claim supremacy over state authority. When the federal government acts beyond its constitutional boundaries, it acts without legitimate authority, and states need not—indeed, must not—enforce such illegitimate commands.

Thomas Jefferson emphasized this principle in the Kentucky Resolutions, arguing that whensoever the federal government assumes undelegated powers, "its acts are unauthoritative, void, and of no force." The question then becomes: who determines constitutionality? While federal courts claim this power, allowing the federal government to be the sole judge of its own powers creates an absurd conflict of interest that the Founders could not have intended.

Historical Precedent and Practice

Early Republic Understanding

The legitimacy of nullification finds strong support in early American history. The Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions, authored by Madison and Jefferson respectively, explicitly endorsed state interposition against unconstitutional federal acts. These weren't radical outliers but reasoned responses from the architects of our constitutional system to the Alien and Sedition Acts' obvious constitutional violations.

Multiple states throughout the early republic era invoked nullification principles. Northern states nullified federal fugitive slave laws in the 1850s, asserting their sovereign right to protect liberty within their borders. Wisconsin's Supreme Court declared the Fugitive Slave Act unconstitutional in 1854, with the state legislature backing this defiance of federal authority. These examples demonstrate that nullification wasn't merely a Southern doctrine but a tool employed across regions when states perceived fundamental constitutional violations.

The Hartford Convention of 1814-1815 saw New England states assert their right to interpose against federal policies they deemed unconstitutional during the War of 1812. This convention, representing the commercial interests of the North, contemplated various forms of state resistance to federal authority, demonstrating that nullification theory transcended sectional interests and spoke to fundamental questions of constitutional structure.

The Philosophical and Practical Necessity of Nullification

Protecting the Federal Balance

The Founders designed a federal system with dual sovereignty, where both state and federal governments would check each other's potential for tyranny. Without nullification, this balance collapses into de facto unitarism, with states reduced to mere administrative subdivisions of an omnipotent national government. Nullification restores the intended equilibrium by providing states with a defensive mechanism against federal encroachment.

Consider the alternative: if the federal government alone judges the extent of its powers, what prevents unlimited expansion of federal authority? States serve as laboratories of democracy and refuges of liberty. The Supremacy Clause Objection

Critics argue that the Supremacy Clause precludes nullification, but this misreads the clause's plain text. Federal law is supreme only when made "in Pursuance" of the Constitution. Unconstitutional federal acts, being null and void, cannot claim supremacy. Introduction

Although the text of the Constitution does not explicitly reference “nullification,” the Tenth Amendment provides robust conceptual grounding for the idea. The Tenth Amendment reminds us that the Constitution is a pact among sovereign entities—an agreement that each state would cede certain, clearly demarcated powers to the federal government. In instances where the federal government steps outside these enumerated boundaries, states, as parties to the compact, can justifiably say that the agreement is being broken.

Furthermore, the very existence of the Supremacy Clause (Article VI) underscores the importance of constitutionality in determining whether a federal law prevails. What is State Nullification?

State nullification is a constitutional theory asserting that individual states have the authority to invalidate federal laws or executive actions they deem unconstitutional. It is not a power explicitly granted in the U.S. Constitution but is derived from a specific interpretation of the Constitution's structure and the foundational compact that created the union.

The Core Reasons for Adopting Nullification

Proponents of nullification base their arguments on several foundational principles:

1. The Compact Theory of the Union: This is the most critical philosophical underpinning. It holds that the United States was formed by a compact (the Constitution) among the sovereign states. The federal government is not a supreme, unilateral authority but an agent created by the states to handle specific, enumerated duties (e.g., national defense, coinage, interstate commerce). Since the states created the federal government and are the parties to the compact, they retain the ultimate authority to judge whether their agent has overstepped its delegated powers.

2. The Tenth Amendment: The Tenth Amendment states: "The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." Nullifiers argue that when the federal government exercises a power not explicitly delegated to it, it is an unconstitutional usurpation of state power. Nullification is the means by which a state "reserves" that power and defends its reserved sphere of authority.

3. The Principle of Dual Sovereignty: The American system is one of federalism, meaning power is shared between a national government and regional (state) governments. Each is sovereign in its own sphere. Nullification is presented as the tool states must use to defend their sovereign sphere from encroachment by the other sovereign (the federal government).

4. The Failure of Other Checks and Balances: Proponents argue that the internal checks within the federal government (e.g., the judiciary reviewing laws, Congress checking the president) often fail. They contend that the Supreme Court, as a branch of the federal government, cannot be trusted to be an impartial referee on disputes over federal power. Nullification is therefore an external check—a right of the states themselves to defend the Constitution when the federal government's internal mechanisms break down.

The Supposed Benefits of Nullification

Advocates present several key benefits that they believe would result from adopting nullification as a legitimate practice:

1. Protection of State Sovereignty and Federalism: It provides a practical, enforceable way for states to resist federal mandates that they believe exceed constitutional authority. This ensures that policy decisions on issues not delegated to the federal government (e.g., education, healthcare, intra-state commerce, land use) can be made at the state and local level, closer to the people.

2. Prevention of Government Tyranny: By creating a significant obstacle to the consolidation of power in Washington, D.C., nullification acts as a powerful deterrent against federal overreach. It decentralizes power, making it harder for any single faction or ideology to impose its will on the entire nation. This is seen as a direct implementation of the anti-tyranny principles central to the American founding.

3. Empowerment of Citizen Voice and Political Engagement: Because state governments are closer and more responsive to the people than the distant federal bureaucracy, nullification allows for greater self-governance. Citizens can more effectively lobby their state legislators to nullify an unpopular or intrusive federal law, making the political process more democratic and accountable.

4. A Peaceful Alternative to Secession and Civil Disobedience: Nullification is framed as a legal, procedural method for resolving disputes between the states and the federal government. By providing a formal channel for resistance, it offers an alternative to the chaos of widespread civil disobedience or the extreme and violent option of secession. It allows for a state to "just say no" within the constitutional system.

5. Encouraging Debate and Clarifying Constitutional Meaning: The act of a state nullifying a law would force a national conversation about the limits of federal power. This process could lead to a clarification of the Constitution's meaning, potentially through the passage of a new amendment explicitly granting or denying the power in question, thus resolving the dispute through the proper constitutional channel.

Historical and Legal Context & Counterarguments

It is crucial to understand that nullification is a highly controversial and legally disputed doctrine.

  • Key Examples: The concept was most famously articulated in the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions of 1798-99 (by James Madison and Thomas Jefferson) in response to the Alien and Sedition Acts. It was later championed by John C. Calhoun of South Carolina in the 1830s regarding tariff laws, and its logic was a primary precursor to the secession of Southern states.
  • The Supreme Court's View: The judiciary has consistently rejected nullification. In the landmark case Cooper v. Aaron (1958), the Supreme Court explicitly stated that the states are bound by the Supreme Court's interpretations of the Constitution, citing the Supremacy Clause (Article VI, Clause 2), which establishes federal law as the "supreme Law of the Land."
  • Major Counterarguments:
    • The Supremacy Clause: Opponents argue the Supremacy Clause explicitly makes federal law superior to state law.
    • Role of the Judiciary: Article III establishes the Supreme Court as the ultimate arbiter of constitutional disputes, not the states.
    • Threat to National Unity: Critics warn that nullification creates a chaotic "veto" power for states, making uniform national policy impossible and potentially leading to the breakdown of the union, as it nearly did in the 19th century.
    • Potential for Abuse: It could be used by states to defy federal civil rights laws and other protections, undermining individual liberties.

Conclusion

In summary, the doctrine of state nullification is advocated as a necessary, constitutionally-derived tool for maintaining the federal balance of power. Its supposed benefits are rooted in a deep commitment to state sovereignty, decentralized governance, and a robust defense against perceived federal tyranny. While it remains a potent political idea and a symbol of states' rights, it operates outside the accepted legal framework as defined by the federal judiciary, which views it as incompatible with the Constitution's text and structure. The debate over nullification continues to reflect the enduring tension in American politics between national authority and states' rights.

Model Response:

The Constitutional Case for State Nullification: Reclaiming the Founders' Vision of Distributed Sovereignty

Introduction

Among the most consequential debates in American constitutional history is the question of who serves as the final arbiter of constitutional meaning. The prevailing modern orthodoxy holds that the Supreme Court of the United States possesses exclusive and unchallengeable authority to determine the boundaries of federal power. Yet this assumption, however deeply entrenched in contemporary legal culture, represents a dramatic departure from the original constitutional design. The doctrine of state nullification—the principle that individual states retain the right to declare federal laws unconstitutional and void within their borders—stands as a legitimate, historically grounded, and philosophically coherent mechanism for defending the constitutional order against federal overreach. Far from being a relic of discredited secessionist ideology, nullification represents the logical culmination of the compact theory of the Constitution, the structural safeguards of federalism, and the natural right of political communities to resist tyranny. This essay argues that nullification is not only constitutionally defensible but practically necessary as a check on a federal government that has consistently expanded its powers far beyond anything contemplated by the ratifying generation.

I. The Compact Theory and the Nature of the Constitutional Union

The most foundational argument for nullification rests on the nature of the Constitution itself. The Constitution was not, as nationalists have long contended, an act of a single, undifferentiated American people creating a consolidated government. Rather, it was a compact among sovereign states—political communities that existed prior to the Constitution, that deliberated independently on its ratification, and that acceded to the Union on specific, enumerated terms. This understanding is not merely an artifact of antebellum Southern politics; it is embedded in the text, structure, and ratification history of the Constitution itself.

Article VII of the Constitution is explicit: "The Ratification of the Conventions of nine States, shall be sufficient for the Establishment of this Constitution between the States so ratifying the Same." The operative phrase is between the States. The Constitution did not spring into existence as a unilateral act of national will; it was established through the voluntary consent of distinct political bodies. Each state convention deliberated independently, and several states—most notably Virginia, New York, and Rhode Island—engaged in protracted debates about whether the proposed Constitution adequately protected their sovereignty. Virginia's ratification instrument explicitly stated that the powers granted under the Constitution, "being derived from the People of the United States, may be resumed by them, whensoever the same shall be perverted to their injury or oppression." This was not rhetorical flourish; it was a formal statement of the conditions under which Virginia consented to join the Union.

If the Constitution is a compact among sovereign parties, then it follows logically that the parties to the compact retain the authority to judge whether the terms of that compact have been violated. This principle is not unique to constitutional law; it is a basic axiom of contract theory stretching back centuries. When one party to an agreement exceeds the bounds of the agreement, the other parties are not obligated to submit to the violation merely because the offending party insists on its own interpretation. To hold otherwise would be to make one party both judge and enforcer of its own powers—a principle antithetical to every conception of limited government.

James Madison articulated this understanding in the Virginia Resolutions of 1798, declaring that "in case of a deliberate, palpable, and dangerous exercise of other powers, not granted by the said compact, the states who are parties thereto, have the right, and are in duty bound, to interpose for arresting the progress of the evil." Thomas Jefferson went further in the Kentucky Resolutions, asserting that "the several States composing the United States of America, are not united on the principle of unlimited submission to their General Government" and that "where powers are assumed which have not been delegated, a nullification of the act is the rightful remedy." These were not fringe positions. Madison was the principal architect of the Constitution, and Jefferson was the author of the Declaration of Independence and the sitting Vice President. Their authority on questions of constitutional meaning is difficult to dismiss.

II. The Tenth Amendment and the Presumption Against Federal Power

The Tenth Amendment provides textual reinforcement for the nullification doctrine: "The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." This amendment was not, as modern jurisprudence has often treated it, a mere truism or a rhetorical appendage to the Bill of Rights. It was a substantive guarantee demanded by the ratifying conventions precisely because the states feared the federal government would attempt to expand its powers beyond the enumerated grants of Article I, Section 8.

The Tenth Amendment establishes a clear structural presumption: the federal government possesses only those powers specifically delegated to it, and all residual sovereignty remains with the states. If the federal government enacts a law that exceeds its delegated powers, that law is not merely unwise or impolitic—it is, in the most literal constitutional sense, void. It is an act without legal authority, a nullity. The question then becomes: who determines when this line has been crossed?

The nationalist position holds that the Supreme Court is the sole and exclusive judge of federal power. But this claim is itself constitutionally problematic. The Supreme Court is a branch of the federal government. To assert that one branch of the federal government holds exclusive authority to determine the limits of federal power is to make the federal government the judge of its own cause. This is precisely the arrangement that the framers designed federalism to prevent. As Jefferson observed, if the federal government were the exclusive judge of the extent of its own powers, the government would possess "a power unlimited in its nature" because there would be no external check on its self-serving interpretations.

The states, as the original parties to the constitutional compact and as the entities that created the federal government, occupy the natural position to serve as a counterbalancing check on federal self-aggrandizement. Nullification is the mechanism through which this check operates.

III. Historical Precedent: Nullification in Practice

Critics of nullification frequently assert that the doctrine was definitively settled—and rejected—by the Civil War. This is a profound oversimplification that conflates nullification with secession and ignores the numerous instances in which states across the political spectrum have effectively practiced nullification or its functional equivalents.

The Alien and Sedition Acts (1798): The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions were the first formal articulations of nullification, crafted in response to federal laws that criminalized political speech critical of the Adams administration. These resolutions were not merely theoretical exercises; they represented the considered constitutional judgment of two sovereign states that the federal government had exceeded its authority. Although several Northern states rejected the resolutions at the time, the underlying principle—that states could formally protest and resist unconstitutional federal action—became a recurring feature of American politics.

Northern Resistance to the Fugitive Slave Act (1850): In one of the most powerful historical demonstrations of nullification in practice, numerous Northern states enacted "personal liberty laws" that effectively nullified the federal Fugitive Slave Act within their borders. Wisconsin's Supreme Court, in Ableman v. Booth (1854), explicitly declared the Fugitive Slave Act unconstitutional and ordered the release of a man convicted under it. The state legislature passed resolutions echoing the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions almost verbatim. Other states, including Vermont, Massachusetts, and Michigan, enacted laws that prohibited state officials from assisting in the enforcement of the federal law, required jury trials for alleged fugitives, and imposed penalties on anyone who attempted to enforce the act within their borders. These Northern states were engaging in nullification—and they were doing so in the service of human liberty against a morally monstrous federal law. This history demolishes the claim that nullification is inherently linked to oppression; it demonstrates that nullification can be—and has been—a tool of justice.

The Hartford Convention (1814-1815): New England Federalists gathered to protest what they viewed as unconstitutional federal actions during the War of 1812, including the embargo acts and the prosecution of the war itself. The convention's final report endorsed the principle of state interposition and proposed constitutional amendments to limit federal power.

Modern Nullification Movements: In the twenty-first century, nullification has experienced a remarkable renaissance across the political spectrum. Over thirty states have enacted laws legalizing marijuana in direct defiance of the federal Controlled Substances Act, which classifies marijuana as a Schedule I drug with no accepted medical use. The federal government has largely acquiesced in this nullification, recognizing the practical impossibility of enforcing its drug laws without state cooperation. Numerous states have enacted Second Amendment sanctuary laws, directing state officials not to enforce federal firearms regulations. Several states have enacted laws refusing to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement. These are all functional acts of nullification, and their widespread adoption across red and blue states alike demonstrates that the principle transcends partisan ideology.

IV. The Anti-Commandeering Doctrine: The Supreme Court's Own Endorsement

Remarkably, the Supreme Court itself has recognized a principle that provides substantial constitutional support for nullification, even if the Court would resist that characterization. The anti-commandeering doctrine, established in New York v. United States (1992) and Printz v. United States (1997), holds that the federal government cannot compel state legislatures to enact federal regulatory programs or require state executive officials to administer federal law.

In Printz, Justice Scalia wrote for the majority that "the Federal Government may neither issue directives requiring the States to address particular problems, nor command the States' officers, or those of their political subdivisions, to administer or enforce a federal regulatory program." This principle recognizes that the states are not subordinate administrative units of the federal government; they are independent sovereigns with their own constitutional dignity.

The anti-commandeering doctrine effectively enables a soft form of nullification. If a state cannot be compelled to enforce federal law, and if the federal government lacks the resources to enforce its laws without state cooperation—which is true in virtually every policy area—then a state's refusal to cooperate renders the federal law effectively unenforceable within that state's borders. This is nullification in all but name. The marijuana legalization movement has demonstrated this principle with striking clarity: when states refuse to enforce federal drug laws and enact their own contradictory regulatory frameworks, the federal law becomes a dead letter within those states.

V. Nullification as a Defense Against Tyranny

The philosophical case for nullification ultimately rests on the principle that political power must be subject to meaningful checks, and that no institution—including the Supreme Court—can be trusted with unchecked authority to define the scope of its own government's power.

The framers of the Constitution were profoundly influenced by the historical reality that governments inevitably seek to expand their power. The entire architecture of the Constitution—separation of powers, bicameralism, enumerated powers, the Bill of Rights, federalism—was designed to create multiple, overlapping constraints on government authority. Nullification represents the ultimate structural check: the ability of the constituent members of the Union to resist federal power that has exceeded its constitutional mandate.

Consider the alternative. If the states possess no authority to resist unconstitutional federal action, then the only remedy available to the people is to petition the very government that is violating the Constitution to restrain itself. They must rely on the Supreme Court—an unelected body appointed by the federal executive and confirmed by the federal Senate—to limit the power of the government of which it is a part. History has shown repeatedly that this is an inadequate safeguard. The Supreme Court has sanctioned the internment of American citizens based on their race (Korematsu v. United States), upheld forced sterilization (Buck v. Bell), and approved sweeping expansions of federal power under the Commerce Clause that would have been unrecognizable to the ratifying generation (Wickard v. Filburn, Gonzales v. Raich). A constitutional system that depends entirely on the self-restraint of the federal government is no constitutional system at all.

Nullification provides the missing check. When the federal government exceeds its enumerated powers, the states—as the parties that created the federal government and delegated specific, limited powers to it—retain the inherent authority to declare such acts void and to refuse their enforcement within their own borders. This is not anarchy; it is constitutionalism. It is the enforcement of the terms upon which the Union was formed.

VI. Addressing the Counterarguments

"The Supremacy Clause Prohibits Nullification"

Article VI declares that the Constitution and laws made "in Pursuance thereof" are the supreme law of the land. Nullification advocates do not dispute this. The critical phrase is in pursuance thereof—that is, in pursuance of the Constitution. A federal law that exceeds the enumerated powers of Congress is not made "in pursuance" of the Constitution; it is made in violation of it. Such a law is not supreme; it is void. Nullification does not challenge the supremacy of the Constitution; it enforces it by identifying and refusing to give effect to federal acts that violate the constitutional order.

"Judicial Review Settles the Question"

The doctrine of judicial review, established in Marbury v. Madison (1803), grants the federal courts the authority to interpret the Constitution. But Marbury does not establish judicial exclusivity or judicial supremacy. Chief Justice Marshall's opinion asserts that the courts have the authority to interpret the Constitution in the course of deciding cases; it does not assert that no other institution may interpret the Constitution or that the Court's interpretations are permanently and universally binding on all other constitutional actors. Presidents have disputed Supreme Court interpretations (Lincoln famously refused to accept Dred Scott as a binding rule for the political branches), and Congress has used its legislative power to effectively overrule Court decisions. The states, as co-equal sovereign entities within the federal system, possess analogous authority to reach their own constitutional judgments.

"Nullification Was Discredited by the Civil War"

The Civil War settled the question of unilateral secession; it did not settle the question of nullification. These are distinct doctrines. Nullification is a remedy short of secession—it is a state's assertion that a particular federal act is unconstitutional, not a withdrawal from the Union. Moreover, the claim that military victory constitutes constitutional argument is dangerous reasoning. The proposition that might makes right is antithetical to constitutionalism. If the constitutionality of nullification depends on historical force rather than legal reasoning, then we have abandoned the rule of law entirely.

"Nullification Would Create Chaos"

The fear that nullification would produce legal chaos—with each state applying different federal laws—presupposes that the federal government is acting within its constitutional authority. If it is, then nullification will not gain traction, because the political costs of defying legitimate federal authority are high. If it is not—if the federal government is genuinely exceeding its powers—then the "chaos" of nullification is preferable to the orderly tyranny of unresisted federal overreach. Moreover, the practical experience of modern nullification movements suggests that the process is far less chaotic than critics fear. The marijuana legalization movement has proceeded state by state without producing constitutional crisis; it has, in fact, produced a productive dialogue about the appropriate scope of federal drug policy.

VII. The Practical Necessity of Nullification in the Modern Era

The case for nullification is not merely theoretical; it responds to a genuine and accelerating crisis of federal overreach. The federal government of the twenty-first century bears almost no resemblance to the limited government contemplated by the Constitution. Through expansive interpretations of the Commerce Clause, the Necessary and Proper Clause, the Spending Clause, and the Fourteenth Amendment, the federal government has claimed authority over virtually every aspect of American life—from the food Americans eat, to the light bulbs they use, to the health insurance they purchase, to the puddles of water on their property.

The regulatory state has grown to encompass hundreds of federal agencies, employing millions of bureaucrats who promulgate thousands of pages of binding regulations each year—regulations that carry the force of law but are never voted on by any elected representative. The national debt has ballooned to levels that threaten the economic sovereignty of future generations. Federal surveillance programs monitor the communications of American citizens on a scale that would have horrified the framers. And through the conditional spending power, the federal government has effectively conscripted state governments into implementing federal programs, transforming nominally sovereign states into administrative appendages of Washington.

In this environment, nullification is not a radical proposition; it is a conservative one, in the truest sense of the word. It seeks to conserve the constitutional order by enforcing the limits that the Constitution places on federal power. It seeks to restore the balance between state and federal authority that the framers carefully constructed. And it seeks to preserve the principle of self-governance by ensuring that the people of each state retain meaningful control over the laws that govern their lives.

Conclusion

The doctrine of state nullification is grounded in the text, history, and structure of the Constitution. It flows naturally from the compact theory of the Union, the Tenth Amendment's reservation of powers to the states, and the foundational principle that a government of enumerated powers cannot be the sole judge of the extent of those powers. It has been practiced throughout American history by states across the political spectrum, from Jefferson's Kentucky to abolitionist Wisconsin to twenty-first-century Colorado. It has been implicitly validated by the Supreme Court's own anti-commandeering doctrine. And it responds to a genuine and urgent need for meaningful checks on a federal government that has far exceeded the bounds of its constitutional authority.

Nullification is not rebellion; it is constitutional self-defense. It is the exercise of a right inherent in sovereignty—the right of the people, acting through their state governments, to hold their federal agents accountable to the terms of the compact that created them. To deny this right is to deny the foundational premise of the American experiment: that government derives its just powers from the consent of the governed, and that when government exceeds those powers, the people retain the right to resist. Nullification is not the enemy of the constitutional order; it is, in times of federal excess, its last and most essential guardian.
